drills.q: Explain why the kernel trick works for SVM's dual formulation but wouldn't apply the same way to the primal.
drills.a: The dual objective and decision function depend on data only through pairwise dot products x_i.x_j, so any valid kernel function can substitute directly. The primal involves w living explicitly in the (possibly infinite-dimensional) feature space, so there's no clean scalar-substitution point the way there is in the dual -- this is why kernelized SVMs are always solved via the dual.

drills.q: A production kNN recommendation system's latency degrades badly as the catalog grows from 100k to 5M items. Diagnose and propose a fix with its tradeoff.
drills.a: Naive kNN is O(n) per query -- brute-force distance to every stored point becomes the bottleneck at 5M items. Fix: switch to an approximate nearest-neighbor index (HNSW or IVF-PQ), trading a small tunable amount of recall for sub-linear query time.

drills.q: Why does Naive Bayes still classify well even though its independence assumption is almost always false?
drills.a: The bias from assuming independence buys large variance reduction -- estimating d one-dimensional per-class distributions needs far less data than modeling the full joint. Getting the argmax class right is a weaker requirement than getting calibrated probabilities right, so decisions can be correct even when probabilities are distorted.

drills.q: k-means produces clusters that look visually wrong -- splitting an apparent single group or merging two distinct ones. What's the likely cause and what would you try instead?
drills.a: Non-spherical, unequal-variance, or unequal-size true cluster structure violates k-means's isotropic-blob assumption baked into minimizing squared Euclidean distance to a centroid. Try DBSCAN (arbitrary shape, handles noise) or a Gaussian mixture model (elliptical, differently-sized clusters) and compare against domain knowledge.

drills.q: A stakeholder points at a UMAP plot and claims two customer segments are 'very different' because they're far apart on the plot. How do you respond?
drills.a: UMAP's objective preserves local neighborhood structure, not global pairwise distances -- nothing constrains between-cluster distance in the embedding to reflect true separation in the original feature space. Validate the claim with an actual statistical test or distance metric computed on the original features, not the 2D plot's visual gap.

drills.q: You're asked to find natural customer segments in unlabeled transaction data. Walk through choosing among k-means, DBSCAN, and hierarchical clustering, and what you'd validate before trusting the result.
drills.a: Visualize first (PCA for linear structure, UMAP for local structure, with its interpretation caveats in mind) to see if groups look spherical/similar-sized (k-means), irregular/noisy (DBSCAN), or nested (hierarchical). Run more than one method -- agreement is corroborating, disagreement is itself informative. Before trusting the result for a business decision, validate against an external held-out signal (e.g. do segments differ on retention/spend not used to form them), not just an internal metric like silhouette score.

drills.q: A stakeholder wants exactly 5 customer segments for a planned campaign, but your clustering analysis suggests 3 or 7 fits better. How do you handle this?
drills.a: Report both: what the data-driven analysis actually shows (with evidence, e.g. an elbow/silhouette peak at 3 or 7) and a clearly-labeled forced-5-cluster result if the business constraint requires it -- don't silently pick whichever k matches the stakeholder's preference and present it as data-driven, since that's a credibility risk if it surfaces later that 5 was decided before the analysis.

drills.q: Two models have identical classification accuracy -- one is Naive Bayes, one is logistic regression. Does that mean their predicted probabilities are equally trustworthy for a downstream threshold-based decision?
drills.a: No. Accuracy only depends on whether the argmax class is correct, a much weaker condition than calibration. Naive Bayes's independence assumption tends to push probabilities toward 0/1 more than warranted (multiplying correlated evidence as if independent), while logistic regression directly optimizes cross-entropy on its own outputs -- equal accuracy does not imply equal calibration, and this matters a great deal if probabilities feed a downstream threshold rather than just a top-class label.
